extracted.intended_audience: college instructors/course designers and middle-school mathematics teachers (in-service and prospective); teacher-educators
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and teaching a discrete mathematics course for middle school teachers using a guided-discovery/problem-sequence textbook. Covers course structure, in-class activities, assessment, and expectations for student work (homework, presentations, exams, and a final instructional module).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparatory work (weekly problem sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A week before each class students were assigned a selection of approximately six to ten (usually consecutive) problems from the notes to work on at home. Students were expected to work on the problems on their own and to bring their results to class, regardless of their state of completion or correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: develop essential concepts and results, practice reading and interpreting unfamiliar mathematical text, and record experimentation, questions, and conjectures to bring to group work. Anti-pattern: skipping preparatory problems or relying on others in class to supply prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-group discussion participation
rubrics_metrics.description: In-class small-group work (groups of 3–4) for approximately 80 minutes to compare answers, solve challenging problems, and develop strategies. Groups sometimes assigned to ensure varied interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor circulates, listens, asks probing questions, and intervenes only briefly to keep groups on a fruitful path. Group work is central to learning; participation is expected and counted toward the course grade (overall participation = 10%). Groups should rotate so students do not consistently rely on a stronger classmate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of solutions (board presentations)
rubrics_metrics.description: After group work, about 50 minutes of class is devoted to whole-class presentations. Each student is expected to present at least two solutions at the board during the semester.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor and students jointly pick which problems to discuss (those that capture essential ideas or show innovative approaches). Presentations are generally voluntary but peers and the instructor may encourage shy students. Students should be prepared to explain and defend approaches; peer critique and debate are normal. Typical distribution: many students present 4–7 times; minimum is two presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graded homework sets (individual mastery demonstration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplementary homework assignments (exercises modeled on the notes) are assigned and due approximately every 3–4 weeks. These graded homework sets are the primary evidence of individual mastery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework must contain carefully written, detailed, logical explanations from beginning to end, using proper notation and terminology. Rigorous formalism is not required, but answers should be more than terse claims (example anti-pattern: 'The function is surjective because every element of the co-domain has a preimage' is insufficient). Satisfactory justification example: explicitly describing domain/codomain and why each element has a preimage. Homework accounts for 35% of the grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exams (midterm and comprehensive final)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two in-class exams (a midterm and a comprehensive final) including computational and short-answer explanation questions that require application of studied material to new situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exam preparation includes review days where students list/define key principles, identify exemplar problems from the notes, create similar problems, and pinpoint confusions. Each exam assesses individual mastery; midterm = 20% and final = 20% of the course grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional module final project (teacher-level module)
rubrics_metrics.description: A culminating instructional module at the level of the students' home classroom on a discrete mathematics topic not explicitly covered in the course. The project has a written component and a 15-minute oral presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written part must include explanation of the mathematical content, detailed lesson plans, worksheets, and general guidance for a teacher. Hands-on investigations and experimental classroom activities are encouraged but discovery-method is optional. Students may work individually or in pairs (pairs preferred to simplify scheduling). The project is assessed and counts for 15% of the course grade; assessment details provided in the project instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall grading scheme / weightings
rubrics_metrics.description: Course grade allocation: overall participation 10%; written solutions to homework sets 35%; instructional module project 15%; in-class midterm exam 20%; in-class final exam 20%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most assessment is based on individual work to ensure independent mastery despite the collaborative in-class format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of mathematical explanations and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: While rigorous formal proofs were not required, students were expected to produce detailed contextual explanations and justifications in both written and verbal work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should avoid bare formal assertions; provide context, definitions (domain/codomain), and clear reasoning. Example: contrast insufficient justification ('The function is surjective because every element of the co-domain has a preimage') with a satisfactory contextual explanation that ties domain/codomain to the classroom situation ('The function is surjective because the co-domain is the 9 students, the domain is the 12 tee-shirts, and we know that every student gets a tee-shirt').

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on small examples, experimentation, and multiple solution methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Early problems begin with small, concrete examples that encourage experimentation and intuition; students are explicitly encouraged to try multiple methods and make connections to prior information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small examples (lists, tables, trees) to build understanding before generalizing. Instructor may suggest representations (arrow diagrams, input-output tables) and encourage multiple representations. Anti-pattern: jumping prematurely to abstract formulae without exploring examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course notes structure (problem-sequence, no worked examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The textbook/notes consist almost exclusively of problem sequences with minimal exposition: low-level questions progressing to more abstract ones, no worked examples, and no solution appendix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes are designed for discovery: enough problems to permit concept discovery without overwhelming. Instructor customizes depth and can replace sections (e.g., induction chapter replaced with applied recursion for this audience). Instructors should expect students to struggle with lack of worked examples and support them via group/in-class facilitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group composition policy to ensure broad peer interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups are sometimes assigned by the instructor and sometimes self-selected; assignment is designed to ensure students work with everyone during the semester and to prevent consistent reliance on a single stronger student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotating group membership reduces freeloading and exposes students to diverse approaches. Instructor monitors groups and intervenes when necessary to keep discussions productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-class facilitation style (teacher role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor circulates among groups, asks probing questions, suggests examples if groups are stalled, and generally avoids providing final answers or dominating the whole-class discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instructor generally observes presentations from the back of the room and allows students to direct discussion; intervention is minimal and aimed at preserving independence and the discovery ethos. Anti-pattern: instructor providing the 'last word' which can inhibit student independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final project topic selection constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Final project must address a discrete mathematics topic not explicitly covered in the course (examples chosen included voting theory, apportionment, probability, expected value, golden ratio, Fibonacci patterns, graph coloring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing a novel topic requires additional research and results in development of lesson plans and classroom-ready materials; projects that were piloted in actual classrooms were encouraged and valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project evaluation criteria used at TCNJ (example rubric for mid-term projects)
rubrics_metrics.description: At The College of New Jersey, mid-term projects were evaluated on 'mathematical accuracy, organization and clarity, and presentation of the project.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides an explicit model rubric: ensure correctness of mathematics, clear and organized written materials (worksheets, directions), and an effective oral or classroom presentation/demonstration.
